strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper benchmarks FECNet on nine datasets spanning three tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), which is unusually broad for an event-based vision paper and strengthens the evidence for generality.

Strong efficiency results: FECNet achieves competitive accuracy with very low MACs (e.g., 0.109G on DVS128 Gesture) and high throughput (~230 FPS), supported by a hardware benchmark table comparing parameters, MACs, and FPS against frame/voxel/point baselines (Tab. 5).
The preprocessing-time comparison (Tab. 3) is a useful and often-neglected analysis, quantifying the cost of converting raw events into different representations.
Ablation studies (Tab. 7, Tab. 8) isolate the contributions of the event-based G&S module, Temporal-FA, polarity input, and the number of events, giving some support to the design choices.

The idea of treating event coordinates as a raw, downsampled 'Event Cloud' and applying frequency-domain filtering for long sequences is a reasonable and potentially useful direction for efficient event-based networks.
weaknesses: Overstated novelty claims: the paper claims to 'pioneer' Event Cloud representation, but space-time event clouds with polarity already exist (cited as [48] Wang et al., WACV 2019), and the claim that Point Cloud methods 'ignore polarity' mischaracterizes several cited baselines (e.g., SpikePoint, EST) that do use polarity. This weakens the framing of the core contribution.

Limited technical novelty of components: D-FPS, EF-KNN, and the frequency-domain Hadamard filtering (Spatial/Temporal-FA) are close variants of well-established techniques (PointNet++ sampling/KNN, GFNet-style learnable spectral filters), and the paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond recombination.

The complexity analysis for Spatial-FA is questionable: FFT along the feature/channel dimension is unconventional, the claimed 'reduction factor of 60' and 'up to 20 times' are presented without a rigorous derivation or wall-clock verification per module, and the convolution-frequency equivalence assumed ignores padding/boundary effects.

Reproducibility concerns: for several datasets (N-Caltech101, CIFAR10-DVS, ASL-DVS, Daily DVS, UCF101-DVS) the authors use their own random 80/20 splits rather than official splits, making direct comparison with published numbers problematic; no standard deviations or multiple-run results are reported anywhere; and the abstract states 'Our code is available at' with no URL provided.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('Pretrainning', 'Experimemt', 'Abaltion', 'spectrum' misspelled, incomplete sentences), and some tables/results descriptions are confusing (e.g., the LSTM discussion in Sec. 4.7.2 appears contradictory with Tab. 8).
Ablations are only run on three of the nine datasets, and there is no limitations discussion; strong claims ('ground-breaking results') are not matched by the reporting rigor.
Action recognition gains on Daily DVS are marginal (+0.2% over TTPOINT) and some comparisons mix different evaluation protocols, tempering the SOTA claims.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: the method is evaluated on nine datasets spanning three tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), which is more extensive than typical point-based event-camera papers.
The reported efficiency numbers are attractive if taken at face value: low MACs (Tab. 5, 6), low preprocessing time for Event Cloud (Tab. 3), and high throughput (~230 FPS on DVS128 Gesture).

The ablation study (Tab. 7, 8) at least attempts to isolate the contribution of polarity, the event-based G&S design, and the Temporal-FA module, and the event-number scaling experiment is a relevant question to ask.
The motivation is reasonable: avoiding lossy frame/voxel conversion while exploiting the temporal coordinate explicitly is a legitimate research direction for event-based vision.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core ideas are largely recombination of existing techniques: learnable global filters in the frequency domain are directly taken from GFNet/FFC [40, 11], and the G&S design is a minor modification of PointNet++/TTPOINT. The claim that FECNet 'pioneer[s] Event Cloud representation' is overstated — space-time event clouds (2S-1T-1P) were already introduced by Wang et al. [48], which the paper itself cites.

The headline efficiency claim rests on theoretical complexity analysis that is not empirically validated. The Spatial-FA module replaces convolution over small feature dimensions (132–540) with FFT/iFFT; the claimed '60x' and 'up to 20 times' reductions derive from asymptotic O() arguments that ignore constants and the fact that batched small-size FFTs on GPUs often do not outperform 1x1 convolutions. No wall-clock or MAC ablation isolating Spatial-FA is provided.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the numbers: the text in Sec. 4.6 states GMACs of 'only 0.12' while Tab. 6 reports 0.161; Fig. 1 reports 230 FPS vs. 229.7 in Tab. 5 (minor); Sec. 4.7.2 states 'FECNet utilizes LSTM for temporal feature extraction,' which contradicts the architecture (FECNet uses Temporal-FA, not LSTM) — presumably a typo, but it makes the key ablation analysis ambiguous.

Comparison fairness is questionable. FECNet consumes up to 10240 events (Tab. 8), while the point-based baselines it claims to beat (PointNet++, TTPOINT, EventNet) are restricted to 1024–2048 points. Accuracy that grows with event count (Tab. 8) suggests some of the reported gains come from a larger input budget, not the architecture; a compute-matched comparison is missing.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a main-track submission: the abstract ends with 'Our code is available at' with no URL, the batch size is 'dynamically set to take full use of the GPU's memory' (under-specified), no random seeds, variance, or significance testing are reported, and several dataset splits are random 80/20 divisions without fixed seeds.

Presentation quality is below the bar: pervasive typos ('Pretrainning', 'Experimemt', 'specturm', 'moudle', 'Tansformer'), informal and imprecise claims ('This implies that critical information you omit in the representations, and you cannot recover or make it up'), and overclaiming ('ground-breaking results', 'pioneer'). The ablation covers only three variants; the individual contributions of D-FPS, EF-KNN, and CES — the claimed technical novelty of the G&S module — are never separated.

No limitations discussion, and the theoretical claim that 'filters in the frequency domain ... [are] mathematically analogous to those derived through backpropagation with the same performance' is asserted without citation or proof.

strengths: Broad and convincing empirical evaluation: the paper benchmarks FECNet on nine datasets spanning three tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), which is unusually comprehensive for event-based vision papers and strengthens the backbone-general-purpose claim.

Strong headline results: SOTA on all three action recognition datasets (notably +16% on UCF101-DVS over VMST-Net), competitive results on object classification, and the best MPJPE on DHP19 among compared methods.

Compelling efficiency evidence: Table 5 shows FECNet achieving ~0.109 GMACs and 229.7 FPS with the highest accuracy on DVS128 Gesture, and Table 3 quantifies that Event Cloud preprocessing is ~10x faster than voxel representations, directly supporting the efficiency claims.

The method has sensible technical motivation: treating temporal and polarity coordinates differently from spatial coordinates in Grouping & Sampling, and using global frequency-domain filters to capture long-range temporal dependencies, are reasonable responses to the identified limitations of Point Cloud-based event methods.

Ablation studies cover the core design choices (event-based G&S, Temporal-FA, polarity) and separately study scaling behavior with the number of events (Table 8), which supports the claims about performance plateaus in prior point-based methods.
Frequency-domain modules build on established techniques (GFNet/FFC-style learnable global filters), so the approach is well-grounded and likely reproducible in spirit.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core components are adaptations of PointNet++-style sampling/grouping (D-FPS, EF-KNN, CES) plus GFNet-style spectral filtering. The main novelty is their combination and application to Event Cloud rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which may be seen as limited for a main-track paper.

Reproducibility gaps: the abstract states 'Our code is available at' but no URL or repository is actually provided. Additionally, several datasets use random 80/20 splits following prior work, and no variance/std over repeated runs is reported, making some marginal improvements (e.g., 0.947 vs 0.953 on N-Cars, 0.824 vs 0.822 on N-Caltech101) hard to interpret.

Comparison fairness concerns: the strongest object-classification baselines with ImageNet pretraining are reported separately, but no recent strong point-based SOTA (e.g., SpikePoint, EventMamba) is compared on the classification task, only on action recognition; some compared baselines are several years old.

Complexity claims are asserted rather than rigorously verified: the '20x reduction' from the Spatial-FA module and the 'repetition of 10^4' figure are derived from rough back-of-envelope calculations; no per-module MACs breakdown or direct convolution-vs-FA empirical comparison is provided.

Inconsistencies and writing errors reduce clarity: GMACs is reported as 0.161 in Table 6 but '0.12' in the text; notation F_G is reused with different dimensions in Eqs. (6) and (9); Eq. (14) defines F_A = F_S · A but writes 'F ∈ R...' for the result dimension; typos throughout ('Pretrainning', 'Experimemt', 'specturm', 'moudle'). The Table 8 discussion is confusingly worded ('FECNet utilizes LSTM for temporal feature extraction, which makes it difficult to capture long-term dependencies'), apparently describing the 'FECNet w LSTM' variant but written as if about FECNet itself.

No limitations section: potential weaknesses such as sensitivity to FPS/K hyperparameters, behavior on very high event-rate scenes, applicability to dense prediction tasks, or the discrete-spectrum truncation effects of the learnable filters are not discussed.

The claimed conceptual distinction from Point Cloud ('does not exhibit permutation invariance') is used to justify chronological ordering, yet the frequency-domain temporal analysis inherently assumes ordered sequences; the interaction between feature-based EF-KNN (which is order-invariant) and the explicit temporal modeling is not analyzed, leaving some design rationale under-explored.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning ten datasets across three tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), with consistent comparisons against recent frame-, voxel-, point-cloud-based baselines (Tables 2, 3, 5, 7).

The paper honestly reports the accuracy/efficiency trade-off of the Spatial-FA module (Table 13 shows ECNet with convolution slightly outperforms SECNet on most datasets), which lends credibility to the efficiency claims rather than overselling.

Beyond standard GMACs/parameters/latency metrics, the paper provides genuinely useful systems evidence: preprocessing-time comparison of six representations (Table 4), a runtime/GMACs lookup table across configurations (Table 12), and measured FPGA deployment results (Table 10), which directly support the edge-deployability motivation.

Thorough ablations covering each proposed component (D-FPS scaling factor, EF-KNN, SFA, TFA, structural vs. input-level polarity), plus scalability-to-event-number comparisons against LSTM-based and PointNet++ baselines (Table 9).

The identified problem—poor scalability of point-cloud-based event networks to large numbers of events—is well-motivated and empirically demonstrated, and Event Cloud preprocessing is convincingly shown to be an order of magnitude cheaper than voxel/rasterized alternatives.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core mechanism (learnable global filters applied via FFT-Hadamard product, following GFNet/FFC) and the PointNet++-style grouping/sampling scaffolding are established components; the contribution is largely their application to Event Cloud data rather than a new methodological insight.

The interpretation of the frequency modules is questionable: the 'Spatial-FA' actually performs FFT along the feature/channel dimension (D_i, e.g., 132 channels per Appendix F), which is a somewhat unusual operation whose connection to 'spatial features' is asserted rather than analyzed; no spectral analysis or visualization is provided to substantiate the claimed low/high-frequency semantics.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos and informal phrasing ('extinguishes the explosion of MACs', 'Without Pretrainning', 'substantiate the scalability'), inconsistent naming across tables (ASL-DVS vs. ALS-DVS; TTPOINT vs. TiPoint), a placeholder instead of a code URL ('available at: .'), and odd usage like citing the DHP19 dataset as a 'Method' baseline in Table 7.

Several headline comparisons are fragile: SECNet's average object-classification accuracy (0.905) essentially ties VMST-Net (0.902) with per-dataset wins and losses; no standard deviations or multiple seeds are reported anywhere, making close margins hard to interpret; the claimed 'factor of 60' complexity reduction is revised to ~20x in the actual network without reconciliation.

Reproducibility is uncertain: code link is missing, key details such as the learnable filter parameterization and training protocol vary per dataset with only partial documentation, and several baselines appear to be reported from prior papers rather than re-run under identical splits (the random 80/20 splits for five datasets without official divisions add variance that is not quantified).

The limitations discussion is thin; there is no explicit limitations section, and claims such as 'ground-breaking results' are overstated relative to what the tables show (strong but not uniformly SOTA results).
The gain in table formatting (e.g., Table 13) is error-prone and hard to parse; the DHP19 MPJPE gains over Point Transformer (69.89 vs. 73.07) rest on a single dataset and single run.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: the method is evaluated on ten datasets spanning three tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), which is more comprehensive than most event-camera classification papers.

The efficiency story is substantiated with multiple angles: MACs/parameter counts (Tables 6, 7, 12), preprocessing time comparison (Table 4), and an actual measured FPGA deployment of the SFA module (Table 10), which goes beyond the usual GPU-only benchmarking.

The Event Cloud representation framing (preserving chronological ordering and fine-grained temporal resolution, avoiding quantization) is clearly motivated, and the claim that representation-level information loss cannot be recovered by architecture is plausible and supported by the UCF101-DVS gain over voxel methods.
The ablation study (Table 8) covers the main components, including the interesting 'Input P' vs. structural polarity comparison, which is the paper's central design claim.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the evidence. The headline claim of superiority is not supported: on object classification SECNet's average (0.905) is essentially tied with VMST-Net (0.902), and it is actually below EDGCN on N-Cars (0.947 vs 0.958). Calling this 'ground-breaking results' and showing a radar chart (Figure 1) that visually implies dominance on seven datasets is misleading. Only on UCF101-DVS and THUE-ACT-50 is the gain substantial.

Limited originality. The core technical ingredients are well-established: Event Cloud representation (Wang et al., 2019a), PointNet++-style G&S, and learnable global frequency filters in the Fourier domain (GFNet, Rao et al., 2021), applied almost verbatim (Eq. 15 is the standard GFNet block). The D-FPS/EF-KNN/CES modifications are incremental tweaks to PointNet++.

An efficiency-performance tradeoff is admitted in the appendix but buried: Table 13 shows SECNet 'generally underperforms ECNet across most datasets' (the convolution variant), e.g., 0.892 vs 0.941 on UCF101-DVS and 6.11 vs 5.87 on DHP19. The main text presents frequency-domain feature extraction as an unqualified win, which is not what the paper's own evidence shows.

Presentation and writing quality are below the bar for the main track: the unresolved code URL in the abstract ('Our code will be available at: .'), informal/grammatical passages ('This implies that critical information you omit in the representations, and you cannot recover or make it up through the network architecture.'), typos ('Pretrainning', 'RAMB18 is reduced from 84 s to 39'), and Table 13, whose layout is broken and unreadable (metric rows mislabeled, columns misaligned), undermining a key ablation.

Comparative rigor is questionable. Frame-based baselines are only compared 'without pretraining'; no variance or repeated-run statistics are reported; Daily DVS accuracy is reported to five decimal places (0.9965) with no uncertainty; Table 9's N-Caltech101 accuracies (~46-60) are on a completely different scale from Table 2 (0.824) with no explanation of the protocol change, and the text discussing it is confusing. Recent point-based competitors (SpikePoint, EventMamba) are absent from the object-classification comparison.

The 'scalability' evidence is thin: Table 9 shows modest absolute gains over TTPOINT at large event counts on a single dataset, and the claim that MACs grow super-linearly with input is shown in the appendix (Table 12) to apply to SECNet itself.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: no released code (placeholder URL), batch size 'dynamically set', and several crucial implementation details (e.g., sliding window construction, the ~46-60 accuracy protocol in Table 9) are unclear, which would make faithful reproduction difficult.

strengths: Breadth of evaluation is a decisive strength: SECNet is benchmarked on ten datasets across three tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), covering both static and dynamic, synthetic and real event data, which is unusually comprehensive for this subfield.

Efficiency claims are supported by concrete measurements rather than only FLOP counting: preprocessing-time comparison (Table 4), a server-side hardware benchmark (Table 6), a runtime/MAC lookup table (Table 12), and measured FPGA experiments on a Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC (Table 10) that substantiate the edge-deployability claim.

The ablation study (Table 8) is reasonably thorough, covering D-FPS, EF-KNN, SFA, TFA, and polarity at structural vs. input level, and Table 9 provides a useful scalability analysis of accuracy vs. event number against point-based baselines.

The architectural idea is sensible and clearly motivated: treating the temporal and polarity dimensions of Event Clouds differently from spatial coordinates, and using global frequency-domain filters to model long event sequences at low cost is an appropriate fit for this data modality.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail (dimension schedules, per-dataset centroid configurations, pseudo-code, lookup tables), which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and the paper overstates its contributions. The Event Cloud representation is from Wang et al. (2019a), and the frequency-domain learnable-filter mechanism is essentially GFNet/FFC-style global filtering transplanted to point sequences; the core 'innovations' (D-FPS, EF-KNN, CES) are modest reinterpretations of standard point-cloud operations. The claimed 'ground-breaking results' and 'structural polarity integration' are inflated relative to what is actually new.

On object classification (Table 2), SECNet is only comparable, not superior: it trails EDGCN on N-CARS (0.947 vs 0.958), MVF-Net with pretraining on CIFAR10-DVS (0.757 vs 0.762) and N-Caltech101 (0.824 vs 0.871). The headline Figure 1 presents this as dominance, which is misleading.

The ablations undercut two of the three main claimed contributions. Removing TFA barely hurts performance (e.g., N-CARS 0.947->0.944, UCF101 0.916->0.913), and Table 13 shows the convolution-based ECNet actually outperforms SECNet on most datasets (e.g., N-Caltech101 0.941 vs 0.916, DVS Gesture 0.983 vs 0.989 mixed). The SFA efficiency gain therefore comes at a real accuracy cost that the main text downplays ('does not give too much of a discount').

Reproducibility concerns: for N-Caltech101, CIFAR10-DVS, ASL-DVS, Daily DVS and UCF101-DVS the test set is a random 20% split rather than an official division, and no random seeds, number of runs, or variance/standard deviations are reported for any table. With 1-3% margins in several comparisons, the statistical significance of claimed SOTA averages is unclear.
The code link in the abstract is empty ('available at: .'), so the promised reproducibility is not yet verifiable.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: typos ('Pretrainning', 'Point Tansformer', 'Muti-view', 'Implement Details'), awkward/overclaiming prose ('extinguishes the explosion of MACs', 'critical information you omit in the representations, and you cannot recover or make it up through the network architecture'), and Table 13's layout is confusing with apparently mismatched metric values, making the key SFA ablation hard to read.

Several efficiency comparisons may not be like-for-like: baselines in Tables 6-7 are reproduced under settings that are not fully specified (e.g., input resolution, sliding window choices), and the complexity-reduction narrative (MLP replaced by Hadamard product, 'repetition of 10^4') glosses over that the SFA filters are input-shape-dependent and the accuracy gap to conv is acknowledged only in an appendix.
Missing baselines and comparisons to the strongest recent efficient methods in some settings, and the LSTM replacement baseline in Table 9 is only evaluated on one dataset.
